title: SQL Injection in product search endpoint
description: The /products/search?q parameter is interpolated directly into the SQL query using string concatenation (f-string equivalent). An attacker can inject arbitrary SQL via the q query parameter. Verified: sending 'q='+ UNION SELECT * FROM users--' caused a 500 Internal Server Error from SQLite.
evidence: HTTP GET /products/search?q='+%20UNION+SELECT+*+FROM+users-- returned HTTP 500 Internal Server Error.

title: SQL Injection in admin reports endpoint
description: The admin reports/reviews endpoint uses an f-string to embed customer['display_name'] directly into the SQL query. Although display_name comes from the database (not raw user input), it was originally set by a user during registration, so it can contain arbitrary SQL. If an attacker registers with a crafted display_name containing SQL metacharacters, querying reviews by that name becomes an SQL injection vector.
evidence: Line 80: f"WHERE r.author_name = '{customer['display_name']}'" constructs SQL via Python f-string interpolation.

title: Insecure Direct Object Reference - any authenticated user can view any order
description: The GET /orders/<order_id> endpoint (line 48) calls get_order() which only checks whether the order exists; it never verifies that the requesting user owns that order. While list_orders (/orders, line 39) correctly filters by customer_id, the detail endpoint exposes all order data (items, payment info, refunds) to any authenticated user.
evidence: GET /orders/2 with a customer's auth token returns full order details belonging to a different customer. Code at shopapi/orders.py:48 calls get_order() without checking g.user['id'].

title: Token refresh endpoint bypasses JWT signature verification
description: The /auth/refresh endpoint decodes the supplied JWT with verify_signature=False, allowing an attacker to submit any syntactically-valid JWT (including entirely forged ones with arbitrary subclaims) and obtain a fresh, properly-signed token for that user. This means: (1) any user ID that exists in the database can be impersonated by crafting a JWT with that sub claim and refreshing it; (2) brute-force enumeration of user IDs is trivial. Verified: submitting a forged unsigned JWT with sub=6 produced a valid signed token for user 6.
evidence: POST /auth/refresh with json:{"token": "eyJ0eXAiOiJKV1QiLCJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJzdWIiOjYsInJvbGUiOiJzdGFmZiJ9.bad"} returned a valid refreshed JWT. Code: jwt.decode(token, options={"verify_signature": False}) at line 101.

title: Stored XSS in review body rendering
description: Review bodies are stored in the database without any sanitization (shopapi/products.py line 90 inserts body directly). When displayed in the product page template, the body field is rendered with the |safe Jinja2 filter, bypassing auto-escaping. An authenticated user can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript into reviews, which is then served to all visitors of the product page.
evidence: POST /products/1/reviews with body='<script>alert("xss")</script>' succeeded. Subsequent GET /p/MUG-SPECK returned the raw <script> tag in the review-body div in the HTML response.

title: Remote code execution via pickle deserialization in basket cookie
description: The basket cookie value is decoded and deserialized using pickle.loads (line 20). Since the cookie is not cryptographically signed (it's just base64-encoded pickle), any user can craft an arbitrary pickle payload and set it as the basket cookie. Deserializing a malicious pickle payload executes arbitrary Python code on the server. This applies even to unauthenticated users since basket reads occur before authentication checks.
evidence: basket.py lines 15-23: data = pickle.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(raw)) deserializes attacker-controlled cookie data without any integrity check.

title: Predictable password reset tokens
description: Password reset tokens are generated using random.random(), which produces Python floats seeded from os.urandom but with only ~53 bits of precision, formatted as '%08d' yielding only 8 decimal digits (~27 bits of entropy). An attacker can brute-force the token space (10^8 possibilities) to guess valid reset tokens and change any user's password.
evidence: shopapi/auth.py line 135: token = '%08d' % int(random.random() * 10**8) generates only 8-digit numeric tokens from weak randomness.

title: Insecure password hashing - unsalted SHA-256
description: Passwords are hashed with plain SHA-256 without a salt or work factor. This makes them vulnerable to rainbow table attacks and GPU-accelerated brute force. Modern applications should use bcrypt, argon2, or scrypt with appropriate cost factors.
evidence: shopapi/auth.py line 16: hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest() - no salt, no iterations.

title: Race condition in gift card redemption allows double-spending
description: The gift card redemption flow reads the current balance, validates the requested amount against it, computes a new balance, and writes it back — all without locking or atomicity guarantees. Two concurrent redemption requests can both read the same balance, both pass validation, and both commit successfully, effectively spending the same funds twice.
evidence: shopapi/giftcards.py lines 36-44: SELECT -> validate -> UPDATE without transactions or row-level locks. Same pattern as classic TOCTOU financial double-spend.

title: CORS reflects Origin header with credentials allowed
description: The CORS handler (shopapi/__init__.py lines 44-51) sets Access-Control-Allow-Origin to the exact value of the request's Origin header whenever one is present, AND Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true is set. This creates an open CORS policy where any external website can make credentialed cross-origin requests to the API, potentially enabling CSRF-like attacks from malicious sites.
evidence: Any domain set as Origin header will be echoed back as the allowed origin with credentials permitted. config.py line 9: CORS_ALLOW_CREDENTIALS = True.

title: Debug mode enabled
description: The application is started with debug=True in run.py. In debug mode, Flask serves the interactive debugger on traceback pages, which can expose stack traces, source code, and even allow arbitrary code execution if an attacker can trigger an exception. This should never be enabled in production.
evidence: run.py line 6: app.run(host="127.0.0.1", port=5000, debug=True). Additionally, the search SQL injection triggered a 500 error served by the Werkzeug debugger page instead of a proper JSON error.
